subject: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
Dear list,

I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan. For me its like comparing Windows to Linux and i do not argue about what to use, but seriously:

- Which type of problems are better solved in Stan?
- For which problems do we really need a HMC sampler, i.e. a sampler which avoids random walk? Or when are autocorrelations a problem in Gibbs, but not in HMC?
- Why should I use Stan if I only do a meta analysis with few data?

I am trying to compile some arguments to convince people to use Stan, but I was surprised to see how bad Stan performs for a mixture model (the eyes bugs example) - just as JAGS. So I am starting to think that JAGS altogether does a pretty good job at many problems.

Does it come down to raw speed for large data sets?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: d192bffdecbad89c
messages.subject: Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
I can't give the "best" arguments, but here are some reasons that I like Stan (and its community):

* C-like programming for flow control, data manipulation, and variable scoping
* It always converges for my models (when specified correctly).  No little knobs to turn to get good performance.
* Vectorized functions are very fast. I usually have too-much-data and relatively simple models.
* Distributions have sane parameterization (e.g. Normal distribution: precision vs. stddev)
* Very convenient to install and use with R
* Helpful ecosystem (ask a reasonable question, get a great answer)
* Open Development process (get patches as soon as posted to github)

There are some things that I wish Stan could do, and the Stan group is acutely aware of them (see their TO-DO list)

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 4:21:18 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
Dear list,

I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan. For me its like comparing Windows to Linux and i do not argue about what to use, but seriously:

- Which type of problems are better solved in Stan?
- For which problems do we really need a HMC sampler, i.e. a sampler which avoids random walk? Or when are autocorrelations a problem in Gibbs, but not in HMC?
- Why should I use Stan if I only do a meta analysis with few data?

I am trying to compile some arguments to convince people to use Stan, but I was surprised to see how bad Stan performs for a mixture model (the eyes bugs example) - just as JAGS. So I am starting to think that JAGS altogether does a pretty good job at many problems.

Does it come down to raw speed for large data sets?

I would say it never comes down to raw speed. If you want to focus on performance, it should be effective sample size or effective sample size over wall time. Even then, I think Stan and BUGS calculate effective sample size differently, so doing an apples-to-apples comparison takes some work.

I think our goal is to make Stan the best general-purpose MCMC software, but we aren't there yet, and even if we were it would always be the case that other software would be best for a particular purpose. That said, I think a full comparison is a bit premature because Stan has only been in development for a couple of years and BUGS has been around for a couple of decades I think. So, Stan has a lot of room to grow, particularly in the near future when Mike's RMHMC stuff gets merged in and we can attack harder problems. I don't know if there is much left to do on the Gibbs sampling front, except to derive more full-conditional distributions.

Objectively, Stan (at the moment) can't do models with discrete unknowns (unless you can integrate them out) and BUGS can't do models that cannot be expressed as DAGs. Also, a Gibbs sampler can have a low effective sample size when the parameters are highly correlated. Stan currently has difficulty with parameters with very different scales, perhaps exacerbated when the parameters are highly correlated, but these can often be worked around with model reparameterizations. Also, RMHMC is supposed to overcome these problems.

Subjectively, I feel that Gibbs samplers encourage people to formulate their priors in ways that facilitate Gibbs sampling (e.g. normals, Wisharts, etc.) whereas with other MCMC methods, users are free to choose whatever prior reflects their beliefs. Also, I have long been frustrated by BUGS's mostly scalar algebra approach to specifying models, whereas Stan builds on Eigen's matrix library and the STL. It's not just a matter of wall time, but also a matter of convenience and clarity of specifying models, particularly models with many parameters (e.g. X * beta versus x1[i] * beta1 + x2[i] * beta2 ...)

Those seem like the most major points to me.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
> On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 4:21:18 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
> Dear list,
>
> I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan.

Could you let us know what you're looking for in
a sampling package? We're always open to suggestions
on how to make Stan better.

We like BUGS and JAGS and have used them for years
ourselves!

I'd be very curious to hear about this issue from a user
perspective (and thanks to Eric Brown for already
responding [by the way, Martyn Plummer provides good
advice on the JAGS mailing list, too; I haven't looked
at OpenBUGS or WinBUGS mailing lists]).

There's an appendix in the manual that goes over some
comparisons with BUGS/JAGS on a more technical level.

We've been meaning to run some large scale comparisons
for ages, but we keep spending our time working on Stan
instead. We just recruited a student today that's going
to work on comparisons over the summer (it's a bigger project than it
sounds to do this sensibly, with varying scale of data,
of parameters, of data complexity, of model complexity, the
need to deal for initializations and variance of run
times and effective sample sizes with different starting points,
the decision of whether to use the minimum n_eff as the measure
and whether to measure second (centered) moments for convergence
as well as the first moments, etc.).

For some conjugate models like the Rats example from BUGS
volume 1, we're still finding JAGS a bit faster than Stan (I'm guessing
a factor of 2 or 3 at this point). For some models we're seeing
big advantages for Stan. But until we have more information (see
last paragraph), we haven't been shouting this from the rooftops.

Ben's point about measuring effective sample size is very
important and will be more important with RM-HMC and Geometric
NUTS, which are slower per iteration but much better at mixing
and converging. (And for effective sample size, you have to be careful
with mixture models, because R-hat no longer makes sense on
the non-identifiable components; in general, highly multimodal
posteriors are problematic for most samplers and optimizers,
with more problems the more multimodal they are).

The R-hat built into RStan is more conservative (due to
splitting the chains in half) than in R2WinBUGS or R2jags.
RStan also draws prettier pictures. But that's not a feature of
BUGS or JAGS. You can use our posterior analysis with BUGS/JAGS
output or vice-versa.

Here's a list of some issues off the top of my head:

One, Stan declares and types its variables and provides more
extensive warning messages for errors. This is not a small
consideration when developing complex models. I find the types
and declarations make the models (and error messages) more
understandable. BUGS models can be used with any of the nodes
as parameters with the decision made at runtime; this makes a
single BUGS model more flexible.

As to syntax/operations, I also like our MATLAB-like
matrix operations. We'll be vectorizing almost all of the
operations in the language in the coming months.

Two, Stan is more imperative. Local variables can be reused
and sums can be accumulated in loops. You can directly code
your (perhaps not built into Stan) log probability function
with mathematical functions and the lp__ variable. This lets
you encode the functionality in JAGS's GLM module directly
in a Stan model.

Two point Five, Stan lets you specify the joint probability
or the posterior or anything in between -- as long as the
log probability function is proportional to the posterior, you're
OK.

Three, Stan is currently providing optimizers for the same
modeling language and these will get better. (Warning: Andrew's not
a fan of MAP or MLE estimates.) Stan's flexible modeling language
lets you code maximal marginal posteriors with a little work.

Four, Stan should be much less sensitive to initial values
than BUGS/JAGS. This is, of course, problem dependent.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
If Bugs is solving your problems, no reason to switch away from it.  We wrote Stan in part becuase Bugs was choking on certain problems with complex structure (such as multilevel models with unknown covariance matrices) and other problems that were too big for Bugs (such as our tree-ring model).  And when Bugs doesn't work it's hard to do much with it.
A

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
I've converted most of my MCMC work to Stan, and I've started evangelizing it on my campus. The reasons I prefer it are mainly:

(1) Easier to debug than JAGS. Partly this is because of the error messages and partly because the explicit typing forces me to think more.

(2) I work with some non-standard models that require some fiddling to build the likelihoods. For example, experience weighted attraction models of learning need some looping to compute memory effects, and those are rather slow in JAGS, but lightning fast in Stan. Ordered logistic models also are much faster in Stan, but rather a pain in JAGS.

(3) I don't like conjugate priors! Stan frees me to use the priors I want for inference, not the priors I need for estimation.

All that said, missing data imputation is quite a chore in Stan. I expect as array slicing gets added, it'll be easier.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
parts:
Hi!

I am interested in the user perspective as I want to convince other people to switch to Stan. The bigger the community the better. A comparison between the samplers is indeed a bigger project, I am looking forward to the results of your student.

I agree with the points raised so far, i.e. not being forced to think in terms of a DAG makes life a lot easier.

If I understood you guys correctly, then in Stan there is no advantage of using a conjugate prior, correct? So I am free to use anything I think makes sense? That's a good point for using Stan as I never like restrictions due to the sampler.

The only thing I really miss in Stan is ode support, but as I heard this is on the wishlist already. Furthermore, I am mostly interested in solving PKPD models which means effectivley to estimate growth rates of exponentials which are summed together. I already coded such a model and it works, but Stan is not awfully efficient here - the ESS is about 1/10 of the total sample size. I was playing with the thought to code some of the analytical solutions as functions in the Stan library. Is there an obvious place to do these extension and what is the best way to use such functions in Stan? I.e. is Stan extensible in some sense such that one can think of writing a PKPD Stan library?

Another feature which would be very handy is to have views into vectors. I.e. in my problems I have to loop over my data because I only need a certain subset of the underlying vector, but as I know the indices I need each time in advance, a view should make it more expressive and possibly faster. For example let v be a vector of length 10, a statement v[i:i+5] with i=2 would be nice to have.

This is (besides ode) only minor stuff and Stan is a great piece of software! I am really looking forward to where Stan is going, especially with this RMHMC...

Best,

Sebastian

On Wednesday, April 17, 2013 3:00:13 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
The only thing I really miss in Stan is ode support, but as I heard this is on the wishlist already. Furthermore, I am mostly interested in solving PKPD models which means effectivley to estimate growth rates of exponentials which are summed together. I already coded such a model and it works, but Stan is not awfully efficient here - the ESS is about 1/10 of the total sample size. I was playing with the thought to code some of the analytical solutions as functions in the Stan library. Is there an obvious place to do these extension and what is the best way to use such functions in Stan? I.e. is Stan extensible in some sense such that one can think of writing a PKPD Stan library?

Could you post such a model in BUGS and in Stan, maybe with comments in the Stan code as to what you would ideally like to be able to do? We would like to support this and almost had a masters student lined up to do it this summer, but he had to take another job because we weren't quite sure what our project would entail.

Another feature which would be very handy is to have views into vectors. I.e. in my problems I have to loop over my data because I only need a certain subset of the underlying vector, but as I know the indices I need each time in advance, a view should make it more expressive and possibly faster. For example let v be a vector of length 10, a statement v[i:i+5] with i=2 would be nice to have.

I am pretty sure that is on the TO-DO list. Also, I've mentioned to Bob about the possibility of allowing EIgen C++ methods be permitted in the Stan language so that people could do v.segment(2,5) or anything else that was defined by a method.

Ben

Neither of these should be that hard. (Easier than the Cholesky

> Hi!

> If I understood you guys correctly, then in Stan there is no advantage of using a conjugate prior, correct? So I am free
> to use anything I think makes sense? That's a good point for using Stan as I never like restrictions due to the sampler.

Not quite. Stan's going to be much better
with posteriors that are scaled like a normal
distribution. Anything with too-fat or too-thin
tails or varying scales will cause a problem. See
the section of the manual on reparameterization and
particularly Radford Neal's funnel example for a simple
illustration.

RM-HMC won't have that problem (except in very extreme
cases). It makes short work of the funnel.
